title: Why scaling is hard: the fundamental forces that make big companies slower but stronger
summary: Jason Cohen explains why founders can't run a 500-person company like a 50-person one. Two forces drive it: rare things become common, and complexity exceeds human comprehension. He walks through consequences for team robustness, predictability, materiality thresholds, recruiting, communication, infrastructure and risk.

principles.text: At scale, rare events become daily events, so manual handling must be replaced by new processes.
principles.quote: Rare things are difficult to predict, and typically difficult to prevent. Before scale, they are, well, rare, so this doesn't matter; they can be handled manually. But when they start happening daily, new processes become necessary.

principles.text: A team of one is fast but brittle; at scale you trade per-person productivity for continuity.
principles.quote: So a team of one is fast, but brittle. When you're small, this is a good trade-off, because speed is critical for combating the things that are constantly about to kill the company

principles.text: Robustness always costs more than expected, in people and in infrastructure.
principles.quote: Robustness always carries a cost. Whether it's running four servers instead of one, or a team of four instead of one, you trade local inefficiency for whole-company continuity.

principles.text: Large companies need predictability because hiring and launches have long lead times; it is an advantage of scale, not a bureaucratic excuse.
principles.quote: Therefore, we have to predict the demand for technical support four to six months in advance, because we need to be hiring for that right now.

principles.text: The bigger the company, the higher the materiality threshold: projects must be big enough to move the business, or they are failures.
principles.quote: This principle is called the "Materiality Threshold," i.e. the minimum contribution a project must deliver, for the project to materially affect the business.

principles.text: Communicating to hundreds requires simple messages repeated in many formats, times and voices; complex messages can't reach everyone.
principles.quote: The answer is: Repeating simple messages.
